title: Machine learning predicts timing and fault-state evolution in meter-scale laboratory earthquakes
summary: A Random Forest using a network representation of acoustic-emission event catalogs predicted the timing of meter-scale laboratory mainshocks from tens of seconds to milliseconds ahead (test-set log R²=0.84). Feature analysis found systematic changes in event intervals and seismic moments as failure approached; comparison with dynamic simulations led the authors to infer that acoustic emissions indirectly encode stress evolution on creeping fault patches. This is a laboratory-scale result, not a validated method for forecasting natural earthquakes.
ai_technology: Random Forest machine-learning model; deep-learning comparison model
organization: Kyoto University; Disaster Prevention Research Institute, Kyoto University

evidence.tested: A Random Forest using a network representation of acoustic-emission event catalogs predicted the timing of meter-scale laboratory mainshocks from tens of seconds to milliseconds ahead (test-set log R²=0.84).
evidence.unknown: This is one meter-scale rock-friction experiment (experiment LB12-011) and a corresponding numerical model; forecast skill varies with foreshock density and cannot be generalized to natural earthquakes. The article was corrected on 2026-02-02 to replace an uncorrected proof PDF; the correction says it did not describe a scientific-result change.
evidence.ai_role: The Random Forest model made the time-to-failure predictions from the event catalog; the authors analyzed predictive features and compared the results to dynamic simulations to infer that catalog signals encode evolving fault state. The machine-learning analysis is the core result, not merely automated event detection.
